triage.reason: Acute focal neurologic deficit with a time-critical workup and many mimics; excellent interview, exam and imaging case.

Family history of stroke or TIA

chief_complaints.text: My face feels droopy on one side
My arm went weak all of a sudden
My speech is slurred and I can't get my words out
I suddenly can't see out of one eye
I feel dizzy and can't keep my balance
I have the worst headache of my life

hpi.onset: Sudden, maximal or near-maximal within seconds to minutes; patients often can name the exact moment
hpi.duration: Symptoms present at the time of presentation; deficits that resolve within minutes to an hour suggest TIA
hpi.progression: Typically fixed or improving slightly after onset; stepwise worsening can occur with large-vessel occlusion or hemorrhagic expansion
hpi.location: Focal, corresponding to the affected vascular territory; commonly one side of the face, arm and/or leg, or one visual field
hpi.radiation: Not applicable; symptoms are focal and do not radiate
hpi.quality: Loss of function rather than pain: weakness, numbness, slurred or absent speech, visual loss, imbalance
hpi.severity: Variable; can be mild (minor hand clumsiness) to severe (complete hemiplegia, inability to speak or walk)
hpi.timing: Abrupt onset, non-fluctuating; may be worse on waking if stroke occurred during sleep

Trouble understanding what others are saying

Severe headache with no known cause

Focal limb pain with preserved strength

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, or generalized weakness rather than clear focal deficits; aphasia may be mistaken for dementia.
Stroke is rare but can present with seizures, altered mental status, or isolated hemiparesis; risk factors include sickle cell disease, congenital heart disease, and vasculopathy.
missing_classic_features: Vascular risk factors like hypertension or atrial fibrillation

atypical.how_it_differs: Risk is increased during pregnancy and the postpartum period; can present with headache, seizures, or focal deficits that overlap with preeclampsia/eclampsia.
Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke with focal deficits; symptoms may resolve with glucose correction, so glucose must be checked immediately.

general.mild: Alert, awake, no distress; may not appear ill at all
general.moderate: Alert but visibly impaired, may need help with tasks or ambulation
general.severe: Drowsy or inattentive, unable to cooperate fully with the exam
general.critical: Stuporous or comatose, may be intubated or require airway support

labs.caveat: Point-of-care glucose is checked in every suspected stroke before anything else; hypoglycemia is a classic stroke mimic and must be corrected first. Values shown are the low range that mimics a stroke.
Anemia can worsen ischemia and may reflect blood loss; polycythemia raises stroke risk.
Thrombocytopenia below 100 ×10³/µL is a contraindication to thrombolysis.
INR above 1.7 (or elevated aPTT) excludes IV thrombolysis; also points toward hemorrhagic stroke or a bleeding disorder.
Prolonged aPTT from heparin or a coagulopathy is a contraindication to thrombolysis.
Renal impairment affects contrast use for CT angiography and drug dosing.
Elevation suggests concurrent acute coronary syndrome or demand ischemia; it does not confirm stroke.
Identifies undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes, a major modifiable risk factor.
Guides secondary prevention with a high-intensity statin.
Only when subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected and CT is negative or nondiagnostic; xanthochromia supports subarachnoid blood.
Red cells that do not clear between tubes suggest true subarachnoid hemorrhage rather than a traumatic tap.
Elevated opening pressure suggests venous sinus thrombosis or raised intracranial pressure.

initial.why: Point-of-care glucose is checked first in every suspected stroke; hypoglycemia is a common and reversible mimic
Anemia, polycythemia and thrombocytopenia affect management and thrombolysis eligibility
Electrolytes, renal function and glucose before thrombolysis or contrast imaging
INR and aPTT must be normal before IV thrombolysis
Detects atrial fibrillation and acute coronary syndrome as embolic sources
Excludes hemorrhage and is the mandatory first imaging step before thrombolysis

initial.test: CT angiography of the head and neck
initial.why: Identifies large-vessel occlusion for thrombectomy and carotid stenosis
initial.only_if: large-vessel occlusion is suspected or the patient is a thrombectomy candidate

initial.why: Looks for concurrent acute coronary syndrome
initial.only_if: chest pain, ECG changes, or cardiac risk factors

initial.why: Identifies undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes
Guides statin therapy for secondary prevention
initial.only_if: not already on a statin or lipid panel is not available

confirmatory.test: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
confirmatory.why: Most sensitive for acute infarction, especially small or posterior circulation strokes, and distinguishes stroke from mimics

supporting.why: Looks for a cardioembolic source such as atrial thrombus, valvular disease or patent foramen ovale
Screens for carotid stenosis in anterior circulation stroke
supporting.only_if: the stroke is in the anterior circulation and CT angiography is not available

supporting.why: More sensitive for left atrial appendage thrombus and atrial septal abnormalities
supporting.only_if: stroke is cryptogenic or a cardiac source is suspected after transthoracic echo

supporting.why: Xanthochromia or red cells that do not clear confirm subarachnoid hemorrhage
supporting.only_if: subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected and CT is negative or nondiagnostic

supporting.test: Magnetic resonance angiography of the head and neck
supporting.only_if: renal impairment or contrast allergy prevents CT angiography

supporting.why: Selects patients with salvageable penumbra for thrombectomy
supporting.only_if: presentation is in the 6–24 hour window

not_indicated.why: Not part of the acute stroke workup and rarely changes management
Not used to diagnose stroke; a normal D-dimer does not exclude it
No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not needed for diagnosis; obtain only if urinary infection is suspected as a mimic

decision_points: Check glucose immediately in every suspected stroke; correct hypoglycemia before attributing deficits to stroke
Noncontrast head CT must be done before any thrombolytic to exclude hemorrhage
Establish the exact last-known-well time; IV thrombolysis is generally limited to within 4.5 hours and thrombectomy to selected patients up to 24 hours
Review thrombolysis contraindications: recent surgery, active bleeding, platelet count below 100 ×10³/µL, INR above 1.7, or recent anticoagulant use
Do not delay CT for laboratory results other than glucose in an unstable patient
Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Ischemic versus hemorrhagic stroke
criteria.summary: Noncontrast head CT separates ischemic infarction from intracranial hemorrhage; the distinction determines whether thrombolysis or reversal of anticoagulation is appropriate.

criteria.name: Thrombolysis eligibility
criteria.summary: IV thrombolysis is considered for disabling ischemic deficits within 4.5 hours of last known well, after hemorrhage is excluded and contraindications such as recent surgery, active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy are reviewed.

criteria.name: Large-vessel occlusion and thrombectomy
criteria.summary: CT or MR angiography showing occlusion of a proximal intracranial artery identifies candidates for mechanical thrombectomy, generally within 6 hours and up to 24 hours when perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue.

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Low blood glucose can cause focal weakness, aphasia, confusion or altered consciousness that closely mimics stroke.
differential.trigger: Any patient with a focal neurologic deficit, especially with diabetes or on insulin or a sulfonylurea

history: Diabetes treated with insulin or a sulfonylurea
Missed meal, recent dose increase, or unusual exertion
Prior similar episodes relieved by eating
Symptoms may fluctuate or improve with food
exam: Focal deficit that resolves after glucose correction
Diaphoresis, tremor or palpitations
Global confusion rather than a clean vascular syndrome
labs: Deficit improves within minutes of IV dextrose or oral glucose
imaging: No acute infarct or hemorrhage on head CT or MRI

differential.name: Seizure with postictal Todd paralysis
differential.why_considered: A focal seizure can leave a temporary one-sided weakness or speech difficulty that looks like a stroke.
differential.trigger: Witnessed convulsion, tongue biting, or incontinence followed by focal weakness

history: Witnessed tonic-clonic or focal motor activity
Tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or loss of consciousness at onset
Known epilepsy or prior similar episodes
Deficit follows the seizure rather than preceding it
exam: Postictal drowsiness or confusion
Weakness that improves over minutes to hours
No clear vascular territory pattern
labs: Elevated creatine kinase or lactate after a generalized seizure
Prolactin may be elevated shortly after a generalized seizure
imaging: MRI may show an old structural lesion or mesial temporal sclerosis rather than acute infarct

differential.name: Migraine with aura
differential.why_considered: Visual, sensory or language aura can resemble a transient ischemic attack or stroke, especially in younger patients.

history: Recurrent, stereotyped episodes over years
Gradual spread or march of symptoms over 5–20 minutes
Positive phenomena such as flashing lights, zigzag lines or tingling
Headache follows the aura
Similar prior episodes with full recovery
exam: Normal neurologic exam between episodes
No focal deficit at presentation
imaging: Head CT and MRI without acute infarct

differential.name: Bell palsy
differential.why_considered: Acute one-sided facial weakness is a common stroke mimic.

history: Weakness isolated to the face
No arm or leg weakness, numbness or speech difficulty
May follow a viral illness
Ear pain or altered taste
exam: Entire half of the face weak, including the forehead and eye closure
Inability to raise the eyebrow on the affected side
Normal strength, sensation and speech otherwise
imaging: Head CT or MRI without acute infarct

differential.name: Peripheral vertigo (vestibular neuritis or BPPV)
differential.why_considered: Sudden dizziness, nausea and unsteadiness can be mistaken for a posterior circulation stroke.

history: Severe spinning sensation with nausea and vomiting
No focal weakness, numbness or speech difficulty
Symptoms provoked by head movement in BPPV
Gradual improvement over days in neuritis
exam: Direction-changing or unidirectional nystagmus that suppresses with fixation
Normal strength, sensation, speech and coordination
Negative HINTS exam in peripheral causes (no central pattern)
imaging: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging shows no acute posterior circulation infarct

differential.name: Subdural hematoma
differential.why_considered: Can present with focal weakness, confusion or headache, especially in older adults or after minor trauma.
differential.trigger: Older adult, anticoagulant use, or recent fall with new focal deficit or confusion

history: Recent or remote head trauma, sometimes minor or unwitnessed
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
Headache, confusion or fluctuating symptoms over days
Older age
exam: Focal deficit or altered mental status
Signs of trauma such as scalp bruising
Symptoms may fluctuate
labs: Coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia if on anticoagulants
imaging: Crescent-shaped extra-axial collection on noncontrast head CT
May be isodense and hard to see on CT if chronic; MRI more sensitive

differential.name: Brain tumor
differential.why_considered: A mass lesion can cause focal deficits, seizures or headache that resemble stroke.

history: Gradual onset and progressive worsening over weeks
Headache worse in the morning or with Valsalva
New seizures
No sudden onset at a definable moment
exam: Papilledema
Focal deficit that does not fit a single vascular territory
Cognitive or personality change
imaging: Mass lesion with surrounding edema and mass effect on CT or MRI
Ring enhancement or heterogeneous enhancement after contrast
Not confined to a vascular territory

differential.name: Conversion disorder
differential.why_considered: Functional neurologic symptoms can mimic stroke with weakness, sensory loss or speech changes.

history: Sudden onset often in a setting of psychosocial stress
Symptoms may vary or improve with distraction
Prior similar episodes
Inconsistent description of symptoms
exam: Give-way weakness or inconsistent effort
Hoover sign positive
Sensory loss that does not follow a dermatomal or vascular pattern
Normal reflexes and no Babinski
imaging: Head CT and MRI without acute infarct or hemorrhage

severity.mild: Small infarct or TIA with minor deficit (for example mild hand clumsiness or slight facial droop), NIHSS low, patient alert and able to walk and swallow safely
severity.moderate: Clear focal deficit such as dense hemiparesis or aphasia, NIHSS moderate, patient needs help with some activities but airway and swallowing are intact
severity.severe: Large territory infarct with dense hemiplegia, gaze deviation, neglect or severe aphasia, NIHSS high, risk of aspiration and cerebral edema
severity.critical: Malignant edema with decreased consciousness, herniation, or hemorrhagic stroke with mass effect; may require intubation, osmotic therapy or decompressive surgery

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe headache with neck stiffness or vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage rather than ischemic stroke

red_flags.finding: Decreasing level of consciousness or new coma
red_flags.meaning: Large infarct with cerebral edema, herniation, or hemorrhagic conversion; urgent imaging and neurosurgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: New focal deficit in a patient on anticoagulation
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for intracranial hemorrhage; reverse anticoagulation and image immediately

red_flags.finding: Coughing or choking with oral intake, or a wet voice
red_flags.meaning: Dysphagia with high aspiration risk; keep NPO until a swallow screen is passed

red_flags.finding: Irregularly irregular pulse or known atrial fibrillation
red_flags.meaning: Cardioembolic source; changes secondary prevention to anticoagulation

red_flags.finding: Blood pressure above 185/110 mm Hg before thrombolysis
red_flags.meaning: Must be controlled before IV thrombolysis; also raises concern for hemorrhagic stroke
Retinal ischemia or central retinal artery occlusion, a stroke equivalent requiring urgent evaluation

complications.name: Hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic infarct
clues: Sudden neurologic worsening after initial stability

complications.name: Cerebral edema with mass effect and herniation
clues: Large middle cerebral artery territory infarct

complications.name: Aspiration pneumonia
clues: Fever and hypoxia in the first days

complications.name: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
clues: Unilateral leg swelling or calf pain

complications.name: Urinary tract infection
clues: Fever, cloudy urine or new confusion

complications.name: Post-stroke depression
clues: Persistent low mood, anhedonia or withdrawal weeks to months after stroke

complications.name: Vascular dementia and cognitive impairment
clues: Multiple infarcts or strategic infarct location

complications.name: Recurrent stroke
clues: New sudden focal deficit during recovery

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, falls or generalized weakness rather than clear focal deficits; aphasia can be mistaken for dementia; higher mortality and greater risk of aspiration and delirium.

Stroke is rare but can present with seizures, altered mental status or isolated hemiparesis; risk factors include sickle cell disease, congenital heart disease and vasculopathy rather than atherosclerosis; imaging and thrombolysis decisions differ.

Risk is increased during pregnancy and the postpartum period; can present with headache, seizures or focal deficits that overlap with preeclampsia or eclampsia; imaging and thrombolysis decisions must account for the fetus.
Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke with focal deficits; glucose must be checked immediately and corrected before attributing deficits to stroke.
Contrast use for CT angiography and perfusion must be weighed against the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy; MRI and MR angiography may be preferred.

key_questions.question: When were you last known to be completely normal?
key_questions.looking_for: A precise last-known-well time; this determines eligibility for IV thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours) and mechanical thrombectomy

key_questions.question: Did the weakness or numbness come on suddenly, or build up over hours to days?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset reaching maximum within seconds to minutes; gradual progression suggests a mimic such as tumor, infection or demyelination

key_questions.question: Which side of your body is affected, and is it the face, arm, leg, or all of them?
key_questions.looking_for: A focal, one-sided pattern fitting a vascular territory (face and arm worse than leg suggests middle cerebral artery)

key_questions.question: Is your speech slurred, or are you having trouble finding words or understanding others?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysarthria or aphasia; aphasia strongly localizes to the dominant hemisphere and is a disabling deficit

key_questions.question: Have you had any sudden vision loss, double vision, or loss of part of your visual field?
key_questions.looking_for: Monocular vision loss (retinal ischemia) or homonymous hemianopia (posterior circulation or occipital infarct)

key_questions.question: Have you had any dizziness, trouble walking, or loss of balance?
key_questions.looking_for: Posterior circulation stroke; isolated vertigo with other brainstem signs is concerning

key_questions.question: Did you have a severe headache, vomiting, or neck stiffness with this?
key_questions.looking_for: Thunderclap headache or meningismus suggests subarachnoid or hemorrhagic stroke rather than ischemia

key_questions.question: Did you pass out, have a seizure, or bite your tongue?
key_questions.looking_for: Loss of consciousness or witnessed convulsion suggests seizure with postictal Todd paralysis rather than stroke

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a stroke or a transient ischemic attack before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior stroke or TIA markedly raises recurrence risk and changes secondary prevention

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or atrial fibrillation?
key_questions.looking_for: Major modifiable vascular risk factors; atrial fibrillation points to a cardioembolic source

key_questions.question: Do you take a blood thinner such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, or dabigatran?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulant use is a contraindication to thrombolysis and raises concern for hemorrhagic stroke

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent surgery, bleeding, head injury, or a fall?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent surgery or active bleeding excludes thrombolysis; head trauma suggests subdural hematoma

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol heavily, or use cocaine or stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable risk factors; stimulant use raises risk of hemorrhagic stroke

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have a history of stroke or early heart disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of stroke or premature cardiovascular disease

reasoning_points: Abrupt onset of a focal neurologic deficit that reached maximum within seconds to minutes
Deficit fits a single vascular territory (unilateral face, arm and/or leg, or a visual field)
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, or prior stroke or TIA
Point-of-care glucose checked and hypoglycemia excluded as a mimic
Noncontrast head CT excludes hemorrhage before any thrombolytic is given
Last-known-well time established and thrombolysis or thrombectomy eligibility reviewed
Atrial fibrillation or another cardioembolic source considered on ECG and echocardiography
Mimics such as seizure with postictal Todd paralysis, migraine with aura, Bell palsy and subdural hematoma considered and excluded

easy: Older adult with hypertension and atrial fibrillation
Sudden one-sided facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech
Symptoms present on waking or witnessed by a family member
Noncontrast head CT shows no hemorrhage and an early infarct in a clear vascular territory
medium: Posterior circulation stroke presenting with vertigo, ataxia and double vision rather than hemiparesis
Patient with diabetes whose focal deficit could be hypoglycemia until glucose is corrected
Woman of reproductive age on oral contraceptives with a new focal deficit
Small or early infarct with a normal noncontrast head CT, requiring MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging
hard: Older adult presenting with confusion or a fall rather than a clear focal deficit
Patient on an anticoagulant with a new deficit, raising concern for hemorrhagic stroke
Symptoms that resolve before arrival, suggesting TIA rather than completed stroke
Stroke mimic such as seizure with postictal Todd paralysis, migraine with aura, or conversion disorder
Large middle cerebral artery infarct with early decreased consciousness and risk of malignant edema
